That on Wednesday. April 27, 1949, the hours of sitting of the house shall be the same as on Tuesday, April 26, 1949, and that on Thursday, April 28, 1949, and every subsequent day until the end of the session, the house shall meet at 11 o'clock in the morning of each sitting day, and that in addition to the usual intermission at 6 o'clock there shall also be an intermission every day from 1 to 3 o'clock p.m.; that on Wednesday, April 27, 1949, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except questions and notices of motions for production of papers: and further that on Thursday, April 28, 1949, standing order No. 28 shall not be applied.
He said: Having stated to the house that it was the intention of the government to recommend at the end of this week the dissolution of this parliament, I think I need not elaborate upon the terms of this motion. The effect of it would be to make today a day devoted to government notices of motions and government orders, and to sit this evening during the usual hours from seven-thirty to ten-thirty. Tomorrow we would sit from eleven
to one o'clock, from three to six, and from seven-thirty to ten-thirty, and the same on Friday.
The last part of the motion has to do with standing order 28, which provides that on Thursdays and Fridays, when the order of the day to go into committee of supply is called, Mr. Speaker leaves the chair without question put. As I stated on Monday evening, it is the intention tomorrow to ask the house to go into committee of the whole for the purpose of passing interim supply for the period of time required to have an election and thereafter call parliament together again at the earliest convenient day. The government felt that if it were to ask for interim supply on Thursday, it should not do so by Mr. Speaker leaving the chair without question put; the motion therefore will be in the ordinary form, so that members will have the right, if they see fit, to air any grievances they may consider to be of sufficient importance to require the attention of the house at that time.
In view of the evident satisfaction of all groups in the house at the prospect of there being this early appeal to the country, I hope it will be the pleasure of the house to adopt this motion and to co-operate with the government in disposing of matters which are urgent.
May I say just a word more. I think it would be the expectation of the house that if this motion be passed, before government notices of motions are taken up today the orders of the day will be called so that such questions as may be appropriate may be put to members of the government.

This house, as with every other free assembly of the same kind, has a system of committees which are set up for the purpose of examining parliamentary business in detail. It is the function of those committees to analyse, in a way in which it would not be convenient for the house as a whole to proceed without taking more time than would be justified, the problems that come before the house. Through the meetings of these committees the time occupied in consideration of public matters can be shortened.
In addition to the ordinary committees there are a number of special committees of great importance. Early in the session there was an undertaking by the government to set up a committee on radio. There was also a reluctant and belated compliance by the government with the demand for setting up of the public accounts committee. There are several other committees which are called upon to deal with important business. At any time up to the day of presentation of the budget there could have been no question about dissolving the house without proceeding with some of these matters; but once the budget was presented-and according to the members opposite, the present one is an election manifesto-it became our duty as members of the house to examine how the money is to be spent, and we have no right to vote one cent of supply until we have the information we require.
Now we are told that the house is to be asked a second time for interim supply. The house has already dealt with interim supply; and that is the regular and accepted practice. The purpose of interim supply is to provide the money which is necessary to carry on the business of the country while the house is still sitting, and to deal with undertakings which cannot be completed before the end of the fiscal year. That is the basis upon which interim supply is voted. It is also recognized that when preliminary supply is voted there is no debate on the details, because the members will have an opportunity to examine the details on a later occasion.

Business of the House
Unless the members had the assurance of that opportunity they would have no right, as representatives of their constituencies, to vote to the government large sums of money which come from the people. The whole idea of interim supply is related to the knowledge that there will be full discussion of the details of the larger amount, that any necessary adjustment can be made without any effect upon the smaller amount which has been voted, and that the rights of the members of the house shall in no way be prejudiced.
But it goes further than that. With the speculation which was rife from time to time, naturally members were anxious to know whether there was to be an opportunity to debate some of these details. On previous occasions when interim supply was proposed, in order that there would not be unnecessary delay in dealing with details, inquiry was made whether there would be an opportunity to examine these subjects in detail later, and the assurance was given that such an opportunity would be given. So far as the house is concerned, we have been told that dissolution is to be asked for on Saturday, so that there is no argument about how long we are to sit. We are told that parliament is to be dissolved -and we welcome that fact; because if anything ever demonstrated the need for an election to vote into power a really democratic government, the present action of the government demonstrates it.
What is actually happening here is that a motion has been proposed which pretends that there is some business before us which it is the obligation of hon. members to deal with. If there is to be any pretence of business here at all, then the government should proceed to place the estimates before the house so that they may be examined, and so that the affairs of government may be put before the people as they should. Let the government call the public accounts committee; we asked that it be called, and we asked it for a definite purpose. What the government is actually doing is running away from its accounting on all these things. But no matter what course is followed, no matter what course-

Those of us who welcomed the announcement last Monday evening that there would be a dissolution of parliament feel that in expressing that welcome we were fully justified. The business of the house during this session has been made very difficult indeed for those of us who want to see the business of the country conducted in a proper manner. I am going to try to stay within the orbit of the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), but I want to say that there are certain matters on the order paper which should be dealt with before dissolution, and I refer particularly to old age pensions.
My predecessor in the position in this party which I now occupy was in large manner responsible for the recognition in Canada of the principle of old age pensions and we of this party have never at any time done other than try to improve the conditions in this regard. I remember that on those early occasions at least my hon. friends to the immediate right were distinctly hostile to the proposal when it was made some years ago.

I am glad to see that there is a change today. There are on the order paper certain matters, other than the budget and the budget resolutions, which should be

considered. I agree that this house should have every opportunity of examining the annual financial statement of the government and in a proper and parliamentary manner voting the necessary supply after an investigation of the accounts. But as to old age pensions, the house should sit until that matter has been dealt with by this parliament, regardless of how long that may be, or whether it defers the general election or not.
Then there is the matter of the ratification of the North Atlantic treaty. I regard this treaty as of great importance to this parliament and to this country, and I think that before an election this house should express its considered opinion on the pact as adopted for ratification by the various countries which have agreed to it.
Then those of us who come from the prairie provinces are most anxious that this house should express itself on the international wheat agreement; for I am of the opinion that our trading relationships are becoming very difficult indeed, and that the matter of the international wheat agreement is of fundamental importance to that great area which some of us represent.
These are some of the priorities. I know that there is a necessity to transfer the oil from the Alberta oil wells to the other parts of Canada, particularly to the other prairie provinces; but while that is of great importance at the present time, and has been given very high priority, I should like to have seen the government undertake these pipe lines of itself: then I would have more enthusiasm for them. The other problems to which I have already referred are of fundamental importance to this country, and should be given the highest priority. We are going to vote to give parliament the right to set aside certain rules in order that these matters may be dealt with. I hope that this parliament will not be dissolved until these matters of fundamental importance to our people, and to our country in international relations, have been dealt with in a proper manner.
I agree completely that this house should have been called earlier, and that we should have had a short Easter recess if we were going to be pressed for time; but in any event we are prepared to do everything we can to facilitate the business of the house. We have not been obstructionists, and we do not intend to be. We are going to support to the fullest extent of our ability the legislation that is in the interests of this country.

It is apparent that there have been some rather serious afterthoughts since the expressions following the announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on Monday night.
Business of the House
I believe that I stated definitely at that time that I had hoped the government would see fit to complete the business before the house prior to dissolution. I have not changed my views one particle since then.
In addition to what has already been said, Mr. Speaker; in addition to all the important legislation that has been mentioned which I should like to see given the highest priority and put through before dissolution, I think the estimates should have been considered and passed. I do not believe, sir, that the dropping of the business of this house and rushing out to the country will smack of anything but indecent haste. I am satisfied it will impress the people that there has been altogether too much manoeuvring for power and position, and not enough consideration of the welfare of the people. It is the duty of the representatives of the people to see to it that the legislation in the interests of the people is completed and passed. Then, and then only, should we go back and ask for a renewal of our mandate. The people are not going to look very lightly upon this business of pausing with shovels in mid-air and rushing off to the country.

We in this group, Mr. Speaker, especially regret that the proposal for old age pensions was not brought forward earlier so that we could put it through. While we look upon it as completely inadequate, it is a most welcome addition to what has already been provided for our aged citizens.
We further regret that the government has not been disposed to stay here long enough to do something to relieve the poor from the effects of the burdensome high cost of living. It is high time the people spoke in no uncertain terms about this very serious omission. We regret also that the government has not seen fit to assure the people that they will stay here long enough to provide assured markets for our products. This is one of the most important problems facing this country. In common with the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), I feel quite certain that the government sees in its nightmares-and it is having plenty of them-visions of very serious times within the next few months.
Finally, we regret very much that the government has not seen fit during this session to assure the people of Canada that they will stay on the job until they have provided an effective cushion against what is almost certain to be a very serious depression within a short time.
I shall say no more except this: We are prepared to facilitate to the utmost the completion of the program that the government

has set forth, so that parliament can be dissolved and the government can go before the people at the earliest possible day. But, sir, we are not going to be a party to rushing out to the country for power and position. We are going to stay until the last of the business has been disposed of.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a word or two in answer to some of the points which were raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), particularly with reference to the supply aspects of the remainder of this session. May I say at the outset that I was not taken by surprise, because I read his speech in the newspaper this morning. Evidently he gave it at a press conference yesterday afternoon.
The purpose of this motion, of course, as anyone can see who reads it-according to the Prime Minister's statement, it is his intention to recommend dissolution of parliament at the end of the week-is to provide an additional seven hours debating time. If one can judge by the time it has taken the house to deal with the measures that have been before it, if we had seventy times seven hours we would not get through the business to which some members opposite have referred as urgent, unless we stayed here until September or October. The purpose of the motion, and the only purpose, is to give the necessary additional time.
As the Prime Minister has indicated, at eleven o'clock tomorrow morning, if this motion passes, I propose to ask the house to grant interim supply.

I will come to that. My hon. friend has suggested that in the whole history of the British parliament there is no precedent for this action. He has not been here as long as I have. If he had been, he would realize that almost identical procedure was followed in April, 1945, prior to the dissolution of the last parliament. Those who were here then will recall that the main estimates were tabled at about the usual time. I have not the date before me, but it was probably the end of February, about the same time as the estimates were tabled this year. As was customary, the estimates were before the members but were not discussed, and the departments were not opened, for reasons that are familiar to all. Before parliament was dissolved in April, the house voted five months' interim supply. The election took place in June of that year, and parliament reassembled on the 6th of September. A further month's interim supply was granted. The main estimates were again tabled and were discussed in the usual way. I do not know 
whether it is proper for me to do so under the rules, but I say now I intend to ask for an additional four months' interim supply.
Hon. gentlemen say that there should be full opportunity to discuss the details of the estimates. I agree with that. But let me say this: In my eight years, almost nine years, as a member in this house, I have seldom found that members discussed the details of the estimates. We open a department, whether it is agriculture or finance or any other; an item is called, and you will find that there is very little discussion of the details of the estimates or of the amount that is voted.

I recall one instance in which the amount of the estimate was criticized as being too great, and no instance in which it was criticized as being too small. In connection with the statement which has been made that there will be no opportunity to consider the details of these estimates, may I say that there will be. There will be exactly the same opportunity that was afforded in September, 1945, to consider the details of every item in the main estimates. If my hon. friend is so confident, as he pretends to be, that he is going to be returned here as leader of the government, he will have an opportunity of changing them. But I think we will find, Mr. Speaker, that the same government will be sitting on this side of the house, and that the same estimates will

be tabled as are now before the house. There will be full opportunity to debate them.
As I have said, the whole purpose of this motion is to afford us a little extra time to discuss urgent business. It has been suggested that the election should be postponed in order to enable admittedly important matters to be dealt with. I think, however, the feeling has been pretty general throughout the country that an early election is desirable; that the people should have an opportunity of indicating what government they want to be in charge of the affairs of this country in the next few years. Even a paper which has supported my hon. friend through thick and thin-and pretty thin some of it was, too- had this to say-and I am referring to an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of April 8:
Let's have it in June.
Talk of a general election in June has been revived. It seems to be the theory of the parliamentary reporters that if Mr. St. Laurent is able to find some encouragement in his Easter tour of the west, and if his followers come back after the recess in a fighting mood, the Prime Minister will give the word.
If only the public interest were concerned we imagine there is no doubt the election would be held in June, because the leaders are in their places, the issues largely are established, one province has no representation in this parliament, and it would be hard to make out a good case for delay.
Then there is something which is perhaps not too relevant, and the editorial goes on:
It seems to us the public interest would be best served by a short, sharp campaign, such as a June date would assure.
Then finally:
We think it is true also that the weighty problems facing parliament, of defence, of finance, of trade, of controls, could better be handled by a House of Commons fresh from the people-and less immediately concerned with party politics than a house that is in its last days.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISPUTES IN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY
speechtext: May I be permitted to direct a question to the Minister of Labour? Has the Department of Labour taken into consideration, or is it considering, any plans whereby it may be able to restore order in the shipping industry in Canada?

subtopic: DISPUTES IN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
As my hon. friend well knows, there is a jurisdictional dispute going on between two organizations connected with deep-sea shipping on the east coast. When I was active in the labour movement the parent organizations usually played some part in the settlement of these disputes. I think that my department has given more time to this dispute than to any dispute since I have been Minister of Labour. As I said the other day, many employers and employees come to my 29087-166i
Inquiries of the Ministry department, to my officials and to myself, for advice. We give them that advice free of charge. But they sometimes go to other people in other political organizations-and I am not referring to the party to which my hon. friend belongs-for advice, and sometimes they pay well for it.
As my hon. friend knows, after the unanimous recommendation of the board we advised both parties to accept it. The employers did, but the other people in their good judgment or otherwise did not. I am one of those who believe that both employers' organizations and trade union organizations sometimes make errors of judgment. The Canadian seamen's union called the men out on the street. I said to a delegation the other day that it is the easiest thing to get workingmen on the street, but the big problem is to get them back to work again. In my judgment, the hallmark of trade union leadership and employer leadership is to see that you negotiate agreements without lockouts or strikes. I think it is fair to say now, Mr. Speaker, that the most powerful and respected unions have negotiated their agreements in that manner. In conclusion, may I say that I have received many endearing telegrams such as one receives only from the communist party; the language is obvious. May I say, too, that at this stage in life I am not going to be a decoy duck for the communist party. In saying that I should like it to be understood that I am not casting any reflections on the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis).

subtopic: DISPUTES IN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a supplementary question? I should like to ask him if he does not consider that this strike again emphasizes the need for a national labour code so that matters of national concern can be dealt with nationally?
While I am on my feet may I ask the minister whether he has any knowledge of the fact that there are serious disturbances on ships at sea? I have a message here stating that the radio officer and the fourth engineer on the s.s. Dingwall have been threatened. I do not know how true that is.

subtopic: DISPUTES IN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that this matter comes under the national labour code. For generations my people have followed the sea and I believe that the captain should be the captain of the ship.

subtopic: DISPUTES IN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY
speechtext: I agree with that.

subtopic: DISPUTES IN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Absolutely, I knew my hon. friend would. When a ship is in jeopardy no one goes to a communist organizer to remedy the situation. It is to the captain that people turn. I have been raised in the school that believed in the principle, "women and children first and the captain in supreme command of the ship." I know whereof I speak.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Two years ago I was in the West Indies. A captain came to see me from the Hamilton Park. This captain came from Quebec and was a very fine fellow. He said he had to sleep with a revolver under his pillow. His nerves could not stand the strain and he was through. If we want a Canadian merchant marine today, we have to return to the principles of the sea that made the British people what they are.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. I hope he will give me just a second to explain it. It is a serious matter. The question was asked from my left yesterday, I think it was, with respect to freight charges on thoroughbred animals moving about the country. I volunteered to him the information that I thought part of the difficulty had been rectified for a year. The facts are these. The Canadian Freight Association has in times gone by given a special rate to these thoroughbred animals-bulls, and so on-which move from fair to fair. An announcement was made that that rate was to be cancelled as of June of this year, I think. In the meantime the position has been altered and the rate has been extended for a year. But those rates also apply to bulls-and I mean imported stuff-that we need badly in this country to improve the calibre of our stock. Nothing has been done with respect to that item. Will the minister look into the matter? It is a serious one particularly in western Canada where we are trying so hard to improve the grade of our livestock. The cancellation of these rates would render it at least difficult, if not impossible, to have service from this fine type of animal. I think I know what the position is with reference to that particular item. Many years ago, I am informed, the railways granted a special rate to thoroughbred cattle as opposed to other cattle, but because it meant a great deal more work and took a great deal more care to transport thoroughbred cattle, it was a more costly movement. Truck competition arose and carried most of the ordinary breed of cattle, with the result that the railways found themselves handling only the thoroughbred cattle and losing to the trucks the cattle which were not so costly to move. Under a section of the Railway Act- I have forgotten which one, but I think it is section 345-the railways have the right to grant a special rate, and this was an exceptionally low rate. Because the competition was such as I have described, they brought the rate back to its former position. Until well into 1943 the pension was only $20 a month. There are, however, certain deficiencies in the bill before us that should be drawn to the attention of the government as forcefully as possible. The Prime Minister today referred to the bill as one that the house would approve. He said the only thing that would be found wrong with it would be that there was not enough in it. He was right. Another shortcoming, and a very serious one, is one to which I called the attention of the minister by means of a question on the orders of the day yesterday. Section 1 proposes to increase the amount of the pension from $30 to $40 per month, but it does not raise the ceiling on a pensioner's income. At the present time according to the act-we will stick to monthly figures although the act is phrased in annual terms-the pension is $30 a month, and the ceiling on a pensioner's income is $50 per month. That means that a pensioner can now draw the full $30 pension and have $20 a month as other income. If he earns anything more than $20 the amount of his pension is reduced so that the total, including his pension, is not over $50 per month. The ceiling of $50 a month, how-

ever, is not changed by the terms of this bill. The result is that the ceiling of $50 remains so that now a pensioner can have a pension of $40 per month provided he has other income of not more than $10. In other words, the pensioner could have $125 a year other income. We remember that figure; it was in existence for a long time. speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 190, respecting oil or gas pipe lines-Mr. Chevrier -Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make my remarks at the appropriate time which, I would gather, is the present. I find some difficulty with the bill. At the outset may I say that I am entirely in favour of the construction of pipe lines. In what I shall say I shall try to be of assistance to hon. members in reaching some understanding of what we are doing.
It may be news to some hon. members that there are more miles of pipe line than there are miles of railway in the United States. That has been the development, and it means there is only one way which has been found suitable to carry oil and gas.
I make this exception by stating that there are certain gases described as top fractions in the refining of oil, the lighter hydro-carbons which are now sold in western Canada in bottles. These are steel bottles, and they are used extensively now in the farming communities. I believe we have had them for only a year or two, but they have a considerable history in the United States.
I built my first house in Calgary in 1912, and I have never burned a pound of coal from that day to this. Those of us who are located near this natural gas are most fortunate and, broadly speaking, we are anxious that other persons should share our enjoyment of this ideal fuel. Generally speaking, however, in my province we are not being so generous as to say to all the rest of you, and particularly to the United States, "Burn this fuel," unless we are fairly well satisfied in our province that we are going to have enough left to keep ourselves warm, to do our cooking, and so on.
At the bottom of this whole matter is one question, namely the quantity of gas available. To that end, in Alberta some time ago we appointed a commission of which Mr. Bob Dinning was chairman. That commission held a number of hearings in an endeavour to arrive at a conclusion as to the quantity. The lowest estimate of proven gas fields at that time was four and a half trillion feet. I believe that estimate was made by Dr.

Hume from Ottawa, whom we all know, a man of considerable reputation as a geologist. However other estimates made went as high as ten trillion cubic feet.
Since that time other large and new reserves have been established, so that today I do not think anyone knows what the reserves in that country actually are. To say that they are immense, or to say that they are equal to anything yet discovered on this planet, is simply to repeat a truism; it is an absolute fact.
So the idea was conceived by various persons-and I believe there are five different concerns seeking incorporation, to which number may be added another man who visited me this morning wishing to make the sixth. Am I correct when I say there are five?

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext: Yes, five applications.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
The minister says there are five, and this man is anxious to make the sixth. Considering this matter we must bear in mind that there is one pipe line of greater urgency, and that is the one which the Imperial Oil Company wish to build from Edmonton to Regina, a length of some 500 miles. Of course to do that they must cross provincial boundaries and that is where the dominion government enters into the picture. Aside from that I do not think at law the dominion government would have any concern with the matter.
Perhaps hon. members would be interested in a bit of history. In 1912 gas was discovered at Bow Island, between Lethbridge and Medicine Hat. Sir Clifford Sifton and Mr. Coste constructed the first pipe line from Bow Island to Calgary, a distance of about 150 miles, although I do not pretend to be accurate about that. In any event it was a long pipe line for Canada.
Prior to that, gas had been used in Medicine Hat, which town was christened by Sir Rud-yard Kipling, on perhaps his only trip out here, as being the place with all hell for a basement. All you had to do to get gas was to put a hole in the ground and the various manufacturing concerns in Medicine Hat owned their own well. I am sure that there are a lot of people in this house as old as I am who remember going through Medicine Hat before the days of electricity-hydro was unknown then-and seeing how it was cheaper to bum gas all day in the gas lights rather than pay a man to turn them out in the morning and on again in the evening. The supply was tremendous and is still ample for the uses in that city.
Finally the city got control of the gas lands around there and now operates the gas supply. I believe it has been sold as low as five cents

per thousand cubic feet. You people in Ottawa burn a gas which is made from coal or oil and perhaps pay around $1 per thousand feet, although I do not know the exact figure. I doubt if it could be produced for less. It must be remembered that artificial gas has not the heating qualities of natural gas and you can see what this means in the west with respect to fuel. The present price in Calgary is in the neighbourhood of 25 to 30 cents per thousand cubic feet and we can heat our houses for about one-quarter or one-fifth of what it costs down here. The company then raised their price tremendously and as a result lost their franchise. We have been doing a little battling from that day to this.
Then the Turner valley field was discovered. I have forgotten the year when old No. 4 well blew in. A pipe line was built from Turner valley to Okotoks, and then another one was built from Turner valley to Calgary. In Calgary we have been getting all our gas from the Turner valley.
I should like to pay a compliment to the Alberta oil and gas conservation board. During the days of the early discoveries sufficient gas was burned in the air to heat and light a city the size of Toronto for fifty years. That will give hon. members some idea of the waste we had at that time. As a result of the activities of this board, not one foot of gas is being wasted. Not only does the gas supply the heat for all the drilling units for miles around; the gas is used over and over again. It is used first for its lifting power to bring the oil to the surface of the wells which average about 8,000 feet in that particular area. It is then put into a Smith separator-that is not named after me as there are other Smiths in the world-purely for expansion purposes, the oil going out one place and the gas going out another.
The gas then goes to an absorption plant where the higher fraction or white gasoline is taken out, and from the absorption plant it goes to compressors. These compressors pipe the gas back into the formation. In other words, if you have 2,000 pounds pressure at the bottom of your well and you have compressors that can put the gas up to 4,000 feet, it then goes back into the ground and again produces oil. The gas that is not burned or sold keeps going around in that circle.	_
The next development was the discovery of huge fields near Viking which supplied Edmonton and the towns along that line. Then came the discovery about a year or a year and a quarter ago of the Leduc oil field. Along with this discovery were tremendous gas discoveries. One result is that today gas
Pipe Lines Act
is being wasted by being burned in the air, but it is the only thing they can do. Then there are the three, four or five fields which have since been discovered and which have added tremendously to the proven reserve which I am sure at the moment amounts to something in the neighbourhood of fifteen trillion feet. Of course that gas will do a lot of heating.
We in Alberta agree that gas should be used elsewhere but only to the point where we ourselves are safe in the use of that which Providence has thrust under our feet.
For the first time we are dealing in the dominion parliament with the export of gas, but in this connection I should like to call something to the minister's attention. I am not sure where dominion jurisdiction leaves off and provincial jurisdiction begins. In my judgment the principle of this bill is good but it seems to me that there should be some central authority to deal with this matter since it is now interprovincial in character.
I should like to call the attention of the minister to a statute which may not have been brought to his attention. I am quite certain that it had not been brought to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when along with Mr. Manning, the premier of Alberta, he gave a press interview at which they both agreed that the export of gas was purely a provincial matter. I refer to chapter 54 of the 1927 consolidation which seems to have been first enacted in 1907. It is called an act to regulate the exportation of electric power and certain liquids and gases. The word "fluid" is defined as follows:
(b) "fluid" means petroleum, natural gas, water or other fluid, whether liquid or gaseous, capable of being exported by means of pipe lines or other like contrivances, and produced in Canada.
Under that act no one can export natural gas from Canada without first receiving a permit so to do. I think that permit is issued now by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I believe I am right about that. This bill has a number of provisions, some of them very interesting, and is an obvious effort to conserve the gas produced for the people where it is produced.
In the city of Calgary we have certain problems among these companies which we are about to incorporate. Provision is made for building a pipe line to our border, and their idea is to carry it beyond the border, the largest sale being in the neighbourhood of Spokane, Seattle, Tacoma, and so on. That seems to be the closest market. There is another bill making provision for the bringing of this gas to Winnipeg, and the bringing of it further east into Ontario is contemplated by that company. I do not know just how

Pipe Lines Act
far they intend to go at this end. But there is provision in that bill that permits so granted may be cancelled at any time. There is provision in that bill that if any person exceeds the amount of gas covered by his permit one penalty, for instance, is cancellation of the permit. Other penalties are, of course, fines. I remember the sum of $5,000 being mentioned.
Under the main bill the idea is to put these pipe lines under the jurisdiction of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. I come back to the oil and gas conservation board of Alberta, which I mentioned a moment ago. I know a little about that situation because I drafted the act. There was a great row before the legislature of the province of Alberta when we tried to bring that about. We were fought by all the oil companies, but I think it is a fair statement to make-and perhaps the hon. member for Athabaska will bear me out-that it is now accepted as a very excellent piece of legislation.
I know, too, that the people of Alberta are anxious, not only to have a common carrier in the way of a pipe line, but that the owners of those pipe lines should be common purchasers. That means that any act of the owner of the pipe line discriminating against what we hear referred to so often as the smaller man will inevitably be done away with. With that, of course, I am in full agreement. We have some fears, however, if this bill passes as it is presently drafted. May I assure you, Mr. Chairman, as I said at the outset, that in the final result I do not intend to vote against the bill, because I know that an oil pipe line from Edmonton to Regina is a "must" at the present time. By trial and error I think we now have achieved in Alberta the best organization on the American continent for handling a situation concerning which the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and its engineers know absolutely nothing. That is not said in criticism in any way. They know nothing because they have had no experience whatever in the matter.
For example, we have a situation which will arise there in the course of perhaps a matter of weeks. We will have over-production of oil, having regard to the refinery capacity in western Canada. The refineries are owned by two companies, the Imperial Oil Company and the B.A. Oil Company. The B.A. Oil Company has refineries at Moose Jaw and Calgary, and the Imperial Oil Company has refineries at Calgary, Edmonton and Regina, but the capacity is limited.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext: Do not forget the co-operative refinery in Regina.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
Yes, there is a small refinery there. I am very happy that they are also drilling their own wells in the Leduc area and are in the oil business. I am glad the hon. member mentioned that to me. We are going to reach the position very soon where our oil production will exceed the refining capacity. What this oil and gas conservation board must do, and will do, is to fix quotas on every well. We have had to do that before. They will have to fix quotas on every well so that each individual who is producing oil will get his share of whatever market there may be.
As I said, this board has had a lot of experience in Alberta, and they have tremendous experience as to the producing capacity of the wells. No doubt most of you have heard the expression, "gas-oil ratio". That means how many thousand feet of gas it takes to bring the oil to the surface where it can be used by man, where it can be refined, and all that sort of thing. By reason of their experience they are in a position to judge accurately, and they know when it is uneconomic to produce. In other words, you do not get enough for your oil for the amount of gas which you produce, and largely waste. All gas in the Turner valley is now rateably purchased by the Royalite Oil Company. It is not known by that name now; it is the Madison Pipe Line Company, but it is really the same outfit. Every person who produces gas there gets his rateable share of the gas which goes into the pipe line, and which is paid for in Calgary.
There is another feature that the Alberta government have very much in mind, and that is the tremendous future of the uses of natural gas, certainly in connection with salt, and the uses which can be made of it in an industrial way. You are all well aware that the government of Alberta built what we call an ammonia plant just outside of Calgary. There natural gas and natural gas alone supplied all the ammonia necessary in explosives manufactured in Canada, and a great deal of the requirements of the United States and Great Britain. That plant was designed by a Canadian chemical engineer, Mr. Richie Donald. I am very happy to mention his name here because United States interests have come up there time and time again, and down in Texas and along the gulf coast they are duplicating the type of plant he built in Canada. It is a great compliment to a Canadian engineer that he is being copied by the best men they have down there.
Today we do not need ammonia for that purpose. It is being used to make fertilizer, and the plant has been purchased by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. Fertilizer from that plant is being sold in

competition with all other companies. It is being sold largely on the gulf coast of the United States, even in spite of the freight rates. Certainly under the Marshall plan a good deal of that fertilizer is going over to England.
I am anxious that the minister should give us some assurance on two points. The first is that these lines will be common purchasers. I can see nothing wrong with that. The second point on which I wish to have assurance from the minister is that the splendid machinery that the province of Alberta has set up in connection with production will not be disturbed. I am not saying for a moment that the dominion, with its board of transport commissioners, is going to take these powers away; but it does seem to me that in this bill we should have some statement affirming the fact that the present method of production may be continued.
In order to operate you must have constant supervision by production engineers to determine things such as gas-oil ratio, to determine at what rate the wells shall produce so that it may not injure the field, that one man may not injure his neighbours. You must have very exacting regulations with respect to the abandonment of wells. I tell you, sir, that when a well strikes water in a formation which a little higher up is producing oil and gas, the laws of nature work. The water is heaviest and is at the bottom, the oil is next and the gas is on top. If you improperly abandon one well which lets the water into the formation where prior to that fact there was no water you can immediately see what will happen. As the gas is withdrawn there is hydrostatic pressure behind the water and it comes up the producing horizon, and in that way you may lose a whole oil field. That has happened in other places and can easily happen with us.
There are two things that I should like to know. I want to know first of all that in my own city in southern Alberta steps will be taken by someone-again perhaps the question of jurisdiction will arise-to see to it, first, that we do not suffer from lack of gas, and second that we do not suffer in the price that we shall have to pay because higher prices may be offered by such cities as Seattle, Portland, Vancouver and Winnipeg, which may force our prices up.
I do not want to delay these bills, but I do seek to impress upon the minister not the necessity of going slowly, because this is an urgent thing-we have to do it-but the necessity of an assurance from him that as we proceed and gain experience we can have a review of this whole position so that the points that I am making can be taken care of.
Pipe Lines Act
I know three of the companies that are ready to proceed immediately. You will not build a pipe line to Winnipeg next summer because it is a slow process. You are building an oil line from Edmonton to Regina. It is a $30 million project and it is a sixteen-inch line. It should be a twenty-four inch line. That is what they wanted to build, but they simply could not get the rolled steel and so they are taking the best they can get and it will be a sixteen-inch line.
Perhaps this has not a great deal to do with it but, Mr. Chairman, I thought you might be interested in it. All oil comes from Turner valley to Calgary now by pipe line. Here is a rather strange thing. Say in the absorption plants there is a lot of white product. You cannot put a partition in a pipe line, so what they do is this. They just shut off the intake of crude and they put the white product behind it, and it goes all of that twenty-five miles, or wherever it is, into the refineries at Calgary, and the division is still there as plain as can be. In other words there is some quality about it which prevents it from mixing. The little bit of white product that is in with the heavier oil is refined by other means.
As I say, I am mentioning these two major points not to delay the matter further. I trust, sir, that you will forgive me for having taken more time than I had intended.

speechtext:
I had not intended to speak at this stage but for the sake of economy of time and in order to give the minister an opportunity to answer the questions which the hon. member for Calgary West asked, as well as the questions that I shall raise, perhaps it would be wise at this stage to make a general statement and to mention two or three more specific matters.
At the outset let me assure the committee that we are desirous of having this bill passed at the earliest possible moment. We feel that it is a most important bill. So far as it provides authority for the regulation by the board of transport commissioners of pipe lines for conducting oil, we think that the bill is excellent. However, there are some things about it which I think the committee ought to weigh very carefully before the bill is passed. Let me say in a general way that the people of Alberta-that is the province that at this particular moment is most concerned with this legislation-do not feel that the bill as it stands provides sufficient protection either to the people in the province or to the oil and gas industries there and elsewhere in Canada.
By wise and effective policies the Alberta government has stimulated exploration and development of the oil and gas fields. It has

Pipe Lines Act
given that quality of leadership which has resulted in the remarkable development that has taken place in the past fifteen years. Moreover, the government of Alberta has very wisely taken every precaution to apply conservation measures designed to ensure three very important needs, namely, first, the fairest possible treatment of all producers in the province, whether large or small; second, the maximum possible recovery of petroleum products from the bowels of the earth; and third, continuous and adequate service to the Alberta people of the products that are brought up from the earth.
It is safe to say that the conservation program in Alberta, as it now stands, is considered to be the finest to be found in America. I cannot go beyond the boundaries of America because I do not know very much about other places, but certainly it applies to America. The best brains to be found in the world in the field of petroleum engineering have been applied to this problem. The minister of lands and mines, the Hon. Mr. Tanner, has applied himself brilliantly to the construction of this conservation program, and to him must go very great credit for its outstanding success to date. He and his colleagues, working in the closest co-operation with the oil and gas industries, have applied the lessons that have been learned over many decades from producers, from refiners and from carriers not only in the province but elsewhere in America. They likewise have learned many lessons from the experience of oil producers and companies within the province of Alberta going back to the early years of the present century-I suppose as far back as 1912, as the hon. member for Calgary West has said. Particularly valuable to them has been the unfortunate experience in the Turner valley, which was the first major field developed in Alberta. For many years no conservation methods were practised in that field. Gas was the lifting power which brought the oil to the surface from as far down as eight thousand feet.
The scramble and rush to get as much oil as possible out of the ground in the shortest possible time to meet the needs of the Canadian people wasted hundreds of cubic feet of a very valuable asset by allowing it to be burnt in huge flares after the liquid petroleum had been taken from the gas. For years these flares could be seen throughout the whole valley day and night. As a result of that terrific waste of gas in the Turner valley, the best experts available have estimated that 75 per cent of the potential oil supply in that field will remain under the ground. If you can just imagine it, only 25 per cent of the potential oil supply will be brought to the

surface simply because of the criminal wastage of the gas which lifts the oil to the surface.
These wells are very deep and, up to the present time, no satisfactory or successful pumping methods have been devised for them. It was as a result of this tragic experience that the present Alberta government, very early in its life, began the business of conserving gas pressure in order to secure the optimum production of liquid petroleum products. Various methods were used which I do not intend to describe this evening, but following the building of the conservation program a non-political petroleum and natural gas conservation board was set up to administer its provisions. As the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) has said, this board has done a remarkable job. They have looked after the needs of the people of Alberta and of the oil industry. They have devised methods of returning gas into the oil structure by what are known as repressuring methods so that it can be used over again for bringing liquid petroleum to the surface without wastage. They have devised also methods of pro-rating production that have succeeded in extending the maximum of justice and fairness to all producers, large and small. They have, without doubt, succeeded in preventing waste and in lengthening by many years the life of the oil and gas fields.
While doing all of this, the conservation program has ensured that the first call on oil and gas production will be for the purpose of servicing the needs of the Alberta people, and of continuing that service for as long a period as it is possible with the reserves that are available. I might add, Mr. Chairman, that the conservation policy adopted has been accepted wholeheartedly by the producers, and the policy has been so wisely administered that further intensive exploration and development has taken place. This has brought Alberta to the admirable position which she occupies today in the production of gas and oil.
There are a great many more things which I could say about this conservation program, but I must hurry on. Let me simply stress that it is essentially in the interests of all of the people of Canada that the Alberta government and the petroleum and natural gas conservation board shall not in any way be interfered with adversely in the continuation and further development of their conservation program. Like the member for Calgary West, I cannot stress that point too strongly. If anything were allowed to interfere, the interests of all Canada would be adversely affected to a greater extent than anyone now might realize. It is for that reason that the people of Alberta are so concerned about this

bill. It is therefore our responsibility as members of this parliament to see to it that nothing in the bill will adversely affect the life of the Alberta oil and gas fields, or adversely affect the interests of the people of Alberta who have first claim on the production of the fields, or prejudice the rights of individuals or producers in the various fields. Likewise, it is just as important that we see that everything is in the bill which is required to give full protection to those measures which are designed and are now being applied to ensure the optimum of life and production of the various oil and gas fields in Alberta, or in any other province for that matter.
This bill has been before a committee and while it was before the committee the minister of mines and lands in the province of Alberta made a presentation, as did the attorney general of the province of Alberta, on the legal phases of the bill. The Hon. Mr. Tanner, who is the man in charge of the development of oil and gas in the province and who has had a long and successful experience in that field, made a rather lengthy statement to the committee from which I should like to quote briefly. I should like to do so in order to show the members exactly how the people of Alberta feel about this program which I say is in danger of being adversely affected if we are not careful about the terms of this bill.
Mr. Tanner says:
Now. to go further with this returning of the gas to the structure: our practice today puts the company in the position where it buys the gas we say it can, reserving or conserving the gas that we need to continue our production and get greater ultimate recovery. Now, that practice has been carried on for years. There is no objection raised by the companies, producers, or anybody else, because they know that over a period of years they are going to benefit. Now, this gas may be returned to the structure for two purposes; either to conserve the gas for future use, or to use it for repressuring purposes. You should have more oil with conservation. Now, let me deal with this briefly: First, we have the return of the gas to the structure; and to me, Mr. Chairman, that is just as essential as anything we can do in production, and it makes all the difference in the long run whether the business is to be a profitable one or otherwise. And if you wish to check on the soundness or otherwise of such a conservation program you have only to take the Commercial Commission in Texas-they are just getting around to this point now; in fact, as a result of their latest legislation they have put themselves in the position where they can carry out this program right to the letter.
He means the type of conservation program which is now in effect in Alberta. He continues as follows:
After all, our position is that of a young producing province and we have been able to learn and to benefit as a result of their experience;
Pipe Lines Act
He is speaking of the people in the various states in the United States, including Texas. Then, he continues:
We in Canada-I speak particularly of Alberta- own 90 per cent of all the mineral rights in the province, and that gives us authority over our own minerals which they do not have in many of the states. From that it will be clear to you, I am sure, that the return of this gas is essential, and that we must have this regulation which provides that a company will buy gas from the fields we designate and in the quantities we designate. In other words, we want them to honour our conservation program.
Those are the words Mr. Tanner used. He is speaking on behalf of 800,000 people in Alberta. The people of Alberta feel fairly sure that the province has the right to apply the conservation methods to industries within the province. But constitutionally, the province has absolutely no jurisdiction over interprovincial pipe lines and hence cannot declare them to be common carriers or common purchasers. It is impractical, I have been told, to make gas pipe lines common carriers as it is possible to do in the case of oil pipe lines, but the people of Alberta feel that a satisfactory alternative to declaring gas lines as common carriers would be to declare them common purchasers. What do we mean by declaring the gas pipe lines common purchasers? Here is the answer. I will try to explain it briefly. If a gas pipe line is declared to be a common purchaser, then the company would be required to purchase gas from all producers in a field if the producers have the gas for sale and offer it for sale at a competitive price. This, of course, is provided that the pipe line extends into and begins purchasing from that field. This provision would be designed to ensure fair and just treatment to all producers in that particular field. Let me emphasize to the committee that, without this provision, there could be no guarantee whatever that all of the producers, large or small, in that particular field would receive fair and just treatment from the pipe line company.
Let me just illustrate. It is perfectly possible in a certain field-for example, in the Leduc field, if that is where the pipe line company intends getting some of its gas-for a gas pipe line company to get control, let us say, of three out of four wells on 160 acres or a quarter section of land, but not get control of the fourth well. If they begin purchasing gas from the three wells of which they have control, but neglect the fourth and just let it go, it is possible for that gas pipe line to drain all of the gas out from under the fourth well and to take that well's assets away from it, and it is possible for them to be sold down the pipe line without any compensation whatever to the fourth well. That is not fair treatment. That is why it is abso-

lutely essential that in this bill somewhere there be a provision to enable the board of transport commissioners to declare a pipe line carrying gas to be a common purchaser, making it necessary for them to purchase from all the wells, all producers, in a field if they penetrate that field and begin to buy, provided of course that will apply-

speechtext: Yes, pro rata of course. In the second place, by declaring a pipe line company a common purchaser, it would be possible for the board to ensure equitably pro-rated production or pro-rated reduction in production if the interests of the field and/or the people of the province require it. It has been argued, and will be argued further I suppose, that the province has the right already to apply its conservation measures even to the extent of declaring the pipe line company a common purchaser within the province. But I say, Mr. Chairman, that there is grave doubt at the very best as to whether the province has sufficient right- that amount that would make it possible to avoid serious and grave constitutional difficulties at a later time.

speechtext: An unchallengeable right.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext: Yes. What the people require, and what they are entitled to under the circumstances, is an unchallengeable right to the declaring of a pipe line company a common purchaser and for the exercise and application of all of these regulations of the natural gas conservation board. There is at least reasonable uncertainty about it; and because of that uncertainty the Alberta people are asking for certain amendments. When we come to the proper clause I propose, on behalf of the people of Alberta, to submit amendments particularly covering this question of common purchaser, and we shall see what happens to them.

In view of your remarks, Mr. Chairman, I shall say little at this point. The hon. member for Calgary West gave an

excellent and clear exposition of the background of oil and gas development in Alberta. As a result, I think he has put all hon. members of the house in possession of the picture so that they have or should have a fairly good idea of what this bill is about. Consequently I shall make only two observations at this time.
First I should like to make it absolutely clear that I am completely convinced of the necessity of a bill such as this which will make it possible to construct pipe lines which will enable the oil now being produced in Alberta to be marketed. I pointed out earlier in this session that the coming big problem -the one which is now upon us in Alberta- is the matter of transportation and marketing of the oil. Those problems can be solved only by the construction of pipe lines. The pipe line which the Imperial Oil is at present starting to build from Edmonton to Regina is an absolute necessity; and the sooner that it can be constructed, the better for the economy of the entire country.
I think, however, this bill can be improved in certain respects. As we go forward through the clauses I trust that the minister will be agreeable to receiving amendments in connection with some of them, particularly to protect the people in Alberta who are probably most directly concerned at the present time and will be most concerned in the future, particularly as to the export of gas. Personally, I have an amendment that I wish to propose. As I say, my chief interest in the matter at this time is the protection of the consumers of gas in Calgary and southern Alberta. I am sorry that this bill is being dealt with at a time when we are rushed, and when everybody is anxious to get through the thing as rapidly as possible. I trust, however, that that fact will not militate against the acceptance of amendments which I think would improve the bill; and I believe it can be improved considerably in some respects.

speechtext:
I think perhaps I should immediately put at rest the minds of hon. members who have spoken, in connection with some of the points which they have brought up. I do not think there is any doubt that the house in general will favour the principle of this bill as exemplified by the three speeches which we have heard from the opposition, first because of the necessity of the bill and next because, in one particular case at least, of its urgency. But I am somewhat surprised at the remarks of one hon. gentleman who has great knowledge of the law, in that he should have any fears at all in connection with the matters which he submitted. That is why I want to rise at this stage to put his mind and the minds

of others immediately at rest. Let there be no misunderstanding about this bill. It proceeds in no way to take over the rights of the provinces or to invade their field. It is a bill of federal nature simply because, as the hon. member for Calgary West stated, the pipe lines extend from one province to another. If it were possible to move the oil within the limits of one, two or three provinces, then this legislation would not be necessary. So that on the question of interference with the Alberta oil and gas conservation board, let me assure the leader of the Social Credit party, and the two hon. members from Calgary, that there is not the slightest intention on the part of the government or in any of the terms of the bill, to interfere with the program of conservation of that body, or with its activities in any way whatsoever. And I do not think it could, even if it wanted to, because this parliament has not jurisdiction so to do.
The hon. member for Calgary West wants to be reassured of two things, the first of which was that these lines should be or will be common purchasers. I said a moment ago to him, when his attention had been momentarily drawn away from the debate by one of his colleagues, that he is too good a lawyer and knows too much about constitutional law to suggest that introducing the element of common purchasers would be a matter within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament.
I say this to him with a great deal of deference. The matter was gone into carefully before the committee. The attorney general of Alberta moved an amendment seeking to make the carriers of gas pipe lines common purchasers. When he and his associates discussed this with me, I indicated immediately a doubt concerning the legality of that position. He said, "Perhaps you are right, but it is a matter which I think should be given consideration." I did give it very careful consideration, and submitted it de novo to our legal officers. They immediately came to the conclusion that not only would it be dangerous but that it was ultra vires of the federal parliament to attempt to make these common purchasers.
There is no intention on the part of the bill to control in any way the question of production or of prices. Those are matters of provincial jurisdiction, and we are not going to enter upon them in any way whatsoever. This bill deals with the transportation and construction of gas and oil pipe lines and the transportation thereof from one province into another. Neither does it deal with export of gas and oil. I did not wish to interrupt the hon. member who spoke a moment ago when he made reference to that very import-
Pipe Lines Act
ant matter; but I should point out to him that this bill has nothing to do with the export of gas and oil. The bill does not touch that in any way. It is a fact that the act dealing with the export of fluid and electricity has something to do with the export of electricity and, incidentally, of gas. But certainly this bill has absolutely nothing to do with that.
The second assurance the hon. member desired to receive was that the people of Alberta should not be disturbed in their control over the production. I can give him the assurance immediately that they will not be. This bill does not seek to control the production. I do not think parliament has the right to do that, and certainly I know of no attempt in any of the provisions of the bill to interfere with control or production. So that the pro-rating of oil and gas, to which he referred, will not be interfered with in any way.
The leader of the Social Credit party wants to have the assurance that sufficient protection is provided to the people of Alberta and to the oil companies. I believe that was the expression he used. I do not think there is the slightest doubt that the rights of the people of Alberta, so far as their natural resources are concerned, are left in the same manner and in the same position after the passage of this measure as they now are. So that they will not be interfered with.
Then, oil companies made representations to the committee. In so far as I could ascertain from their evidence, I think they were unanimous in their support of the bill. The hon. member for Calgary West referred in glowing terms to Mr. Richie Donald. I had a great deal to do with that gentleman during the war years, when I was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply at that time. Mr. Donald was director general of chemicals and explosives, and did an outstanding job for Canada in those years. He has been here to consult the authorities on more than one occasion in connection with this bill, and I believe he is satisfied with its terms.
The hon. member for Calgary East wanted to be assured that the people of Alberta would be protected in so far as the export of gas was concerned. I believe I have sufficiently covered that point.
I hope I have succeeded in convincing the committee that there is no attempt whatever to control prices or production, or to interfere in any way with the operations of the Alberta oil and gas conservation board, or any of the rights of the provinces in connection with their natural resources.

Here are some of the powers given to the governor in council by section 3:
The governor in council may make regulations not inconsistent with this act for giving effect to the object and intention thereof, and by such regulations may impose fees to be paid thereunder by applicants for licences or others.
2. Such regulations shall be laid before parliament within fifteen days after the making thereof-
Then it speaks about proclamation in the Canada Gazette and exemptions and then section 5 reads:
No person shall export any power or fluid without a licence, or any power or fluid in excess of the quantity permitted by his licence, or otherwise than as permitted by such licence.
Then the act goes on to forbid the construction of lines without a licence. Then with respect to licence to export section 6 says:
Subject to any regulations of the governor in council in that behalf, the governor in council may grant licences, upon such conditions as he thinks proper, for the exportation of power or fluid where a right to export exists by lawful authority.
2. Such licence shall be revocable upon such notice to the licensee as the governor in council deems reasonable in each case.
Then there is provision that the governor in council may set out the provisions of a licence and subsection 2 of section 7 reads:
Every such licence shall be revocable at will by the governor in council if the licensee refuses or neglects to comp_ly with any of the conditions imposed with regard to the'supply and distribution of power or fluid in Canada.
Under that statute the government has taken the authority to cancel licences and do all sorts of things with respect to the production and distribution of power or fluid. I think the minister will credit me with saying at the outset that I did not suggest there was a jurisdictional quarrel, but I have been confused by the act I have just been reading. There is no doubt that under that act the government has the right to make regulations and there is no doubt whatsoever that under regulation they could make the export of gas in compliance with the rights of the board to which I have referred. I hope the minister

follows me because I think that is stated rather plainly in the legislation.
It may be that what I have just been reading is beyond the jurisdiction of the dominion government, and I am not going to suggest that it may be. What I am trying to do is to have this problem cleared up. It would be very simple for the minister to give assurance that those who know how to handle this business are not going to be interfered with by those who do not know anything about it. I am not being critical of the board of transport commissioners, but it does seem to me that it would be a great waste of time to set up a technical staff under that board, which will have to be done if that board is going to do the things it is allowed to do, when such a staff is set up already and operating most successfully in Alberta.

My experience with respect to the export of power is quite limited, but it has been the practice for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe)-taking Ontario as an example-to communicate with the hydroelectric commission when there is any question of the export of power from that province. I take it that in connection with the export of fuel or gas the practice will be the same.
Then again the question may never arise. There may never be set up or authorized by this parliament a company with power to export gas from Canada. I presume that when that condition arises it will be dealt with under the act to which my hon. friend has referred.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
Speaking, not as a member of the government but just as a lawyer, may I say that I was very interested in listening to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. In our respective practices we have had to do with matters that are affected by this statutory legislation. I had always been under the impression that in my province the provincial government, representing the crown in the right of the province, had, as owner of the natural resources of the province, the right to say what should be done with them. In my province the legislature of Quebec has said that no one enjoying a licence to cut timber on crown land can export that timber in an unmanufactured condition. I think as the owners of the fee, being vested with the ownership of these forests, they have the right to say that, just as in British Columbia it was held that they had the right to say what kind of people should work in underground mines that were held under concessions from the crown.
They do that not as legislators but as owners who determine how they want their property to be used. When it comes to external trade, of which export is a portion, I would imagine that the federal parliament would have the right of veto, would have the right to say, "You are not exporting anything, no matter where you take it from, unless you get a licence under this act." But I do not think the parliament of Canada would have the right to say to those operating on crown lands in the province of Quebec, "You shall have the right to export wood cut on those crown lands." That wood is simply not exportable. I would imagine it might be the same situation with respect to gas taken from concessions in any other province. I would imagine the province would have the right to say, "We will allow you to exploit these lands provided you do not send the product from these lands outside Canada."

Pipe Lines Act
In that case I do not think any licence granted under federal authority would authorize a concessionaire to export contrary to the conditions of his concession from the owners, that is to say, the provincial government.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext: That is a term of the contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext: A term of the contract, and I do not think, whatever be the terms of the federal legislation with respect to permits, that such a permit could give one holding a concession the right to violate his contract. It might very well be that, although the owner under the contract did not forbid exportation, parliament could say, "We will not allow you to export gas because we have the control of foreign trade, we will not allow that commodity to go out without a permit, and we will not give you a permit." I do not think, however, they could do the reverse and say, "We will allow you to export it no matter what the province, as the owner of the land from which it is taken, wants you to do with it."

The product, natural gas, is an Alberta natural resource, not a dominion one. There has been legislation interfering-
Meaning in other provinces.

Now the dominion government has the right to control the imports and exports of a province. Of

that there can be no doubt. That is clearly set out in the British North America Act, and if that is clearly set out why should that power be limited by asking the written consent of the province to do thus and so. That is the main objection.
Here is the point, and I think it is the point at which the hon. member for Calgary West was aiming, and on which I have not been satisfied as yet. Let us say a pipe line company is organized and a pipe line built to convey gas out of the province of Alberta to the province of Manitoba. It begins to operate under this act as it now stands, and let us say it goes into the Kinsella field in Alberta and begins to purchase gas for transportation out of the province. The petroleum and natural gases conservation board find that the situation demands the return of that gas to the structure for conservation purposes, and they so order, but the gas is being purchased by the pipe line company under this act, and the dominion government, through the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, is the only one that can regulate the movement of that gas out of Alberta and into Manitoba.
What we want to know is, will the order of the conservation board apply? Will it not be interfered with? Will it be possible under the act as it stands for them to say that the gas will go back into repressure so as to make possible the optimum recovery of liquid petroleum, or will it be possible for the company to flout the order of the board and say, "We are going to take this out because the act says we can"?
